toc.title: All of our states are normal
Some people are not safety cues
When you can't receive the safety that's there
Build your safety state, then listen to what you need
When people aren't working, turn elsewhere

blocks.p: A listener sent me a message about family and safety cues. She wrote:

q: The problem I'm having is that my safety cues (in my normal state) would be family or close friends, like I call mom, etc. but it's like they feel so closed off and I don't feel a sense of relief or safe as I normally would. So that's confusing to me.

blocks.p: I don't know her, so I'm not talking about her specifically. When I say "you," I'm talking in general.

blocks.h: All of our states are normal

blocks.p: First, I think by "normal state" she means the safety state. But all of our states are normal. The safety state is normal. Flight and fight are normal. Shutdown is normal. Even freeze is normal. They all evolved within us over a very long time, to increase our chances of survival or to optimize our resources based on what's happening in any given situation.
The safety state might feel better, but it's no more normal than the other states. That's maybe me nitpicking, but it's a way to think about things a little differently, with less judgment.
So what she's describing is that the typical interpersonal safety cues, the ones from other people, don't feel like safety cues when she's dysregulated. There are two things to address here.

blocks.h: Some people are not safety cues

blocks.p: I don't think this is what she's saying, but it's worth saying: some people are flat out not safety cues. Some people give you danger cues. They might be aggressive, or super anxious, or very withdrawn and shut down. All of these can take us away from our own safety state. They can be mildly to overtly dysregulating.

So people you think should be safety cues, like a spouse or significant other, children, or parents, might be people you'd want to go to to feel safe. But the reality is, they might not be that person. If you're hoping or expecting someone to be a safety cue and they're not, that's just the way it is.

blocks.h: When you can't receive the safety that's there

blocks.p: The other side of this is that the people in your life are safety cues, but you're unable to receive them.

When you're in your safety state, you can receive them. It's probably not hard to be close to someone, to hug, to smile, to make eye contact. But when you're in a dysregulated defensive state, flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze, it's really hard to accept safety cues. It's not something you choose. It's all unconscious, done through neuroception. If you're not in your safety state, it's hard to detect safety even when it's there.
It might help to think of it this way: whatever state you're in becomes your filter for the world.

If you're in a safety state, the world sends its cues at you, they pass through the filter, and they get to you. You'll probably handle things more calmly and more confidently, and you'll feel more connected. That's what the safety state does. Especially if you're strongly anchored in your safety state, you'll be able to maintain those experiences, even with people who challenge it. When someone sends you a cue of slight defensive activation, your safety state filters it, and you have empathy. You may be able to relate. You might be able to help them problem solve.

That's different from filtering the world through a defensive state. If you're in flight or fight, you filter the world's cues through a lens of danger. You're already anxious, or aggressive, or both. So no matter what the world sends at you, even the people you care about, when they say something, or smile, or hug you, it passes through that filter of flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze.

They haven't changed on their end. But the signals they're sending come through your defensive state's filter, and that changes how you receive them. They didn't say it differently or intend it differently. On your end, you're receiving it differently.

Deb Dana put it simply when she was on the podcast: "There have to be more cues of safety than danger in order for me to move into ventral." ([Episode 29](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c))

blocks.h: Build your safety state, then listen to what you need

blocks.p: So the people in your life can still be safety cues. But on your end, it's up to you to practice anchoring in safety and build the strength of your safety state. As you do that, your defensive states become more tolerable. Your safety state helps keep the intensity of your defensive state at a minimum. It softens it.

Then you can anchor in safety, allow a little of that defensive activation, and listen to what you need. Maybe you need a hug, and you'll be able to say, "Hey, I'm really stressed out. I need a hug." Or maybe you realize you need to be alone, and you tell the people in your life, "I care about you. I'm not able to receive it right now. Just give me some time to be alone and quiet, and I'll come to you when I'm ready."

That requires some self-regulation first. If you have enough of it, you can listen to what you need and speak confidently about it with other people. Not demanding it, just telling them where you're at, creating that healthy boundary, and letting them know what to expect from you.

That's the ideal, and it's something to work toward. It doesn't happen overnight. Building the strength of your safety state takes a while, but it's super important in all of this self-development and trauma recovery.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.h: When people aren't working, turn elsewhere

blocks.p: Ideally, you have people in your life, or pets, that you receive safety cues from. Fantastic. But if you're too dysregulated to receive interpersonal safety cues, you can rely on other avenues.

One of those is environmental safety cues. If being with people isn't working out for you, receive safety from the environment instead. I really encourage you to identify a safety spot in your home: a place you can go where you feel more grounded and more connected, more anchored in your safety state.

If you can't get it from people, turn to the environment. If you can't get it from the environment, turn to movement, music, or the thoughts in your mind. There are a bunch of different ways to anchor in safety.
